questions.q: What is the key difference between a repository secret and an environment secret in GitHub Actions?
options: There is no difference, they are the same feature with two names
An environment secret is scoped to a named environment and only available to jobs targeting it, letting you keep a production key pair separate from a lower-sandbox one within the same repo
Repository secrets can only hold numbers, environment secrets can hold any string
Environment secrets are visible in the UI after creation, repository secrets are not
questions.explain: Environment secrets add a scoping layer tied to a named environment (like a production environment), letting different environments within one repository hold separate, non-overlapping secrets.

questions.q: What does GitHub Actions' automatic secret masking actually protect against?
options: Every possible way a secret value could end up in a log, with no exceptions
It prevents secrets from ever being used by a workflow at all
It automatically rotates the secret after each use
Only an exact match of the configured secret's value in step output -- a transformed version (e.g. base64-encoded) can still leak through unmasked
questions.explain: Masking replaces an exact string match with *** in logs, but a transformed version of that same secret (re-encoded, reformatted) can slip past masking -- which is why this lesson still recommends deleting temporary secret files immediately.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a lower-sandbox CI job has no legitimate reason to be able to read the production JWT key?
options: Because of least privilege -- a secret or credential should be accessible only to the jobs that specifically need it, limiting the blast radius if something goes wrong
Because sandbox jobs cannot technically read any secrets at all
Because production secrets are stored in a different programming language
There is no real reason; access should always be shared as widely as possible
questions.explain: Least privilege means scoping access narrowly -- a sandbox-targeting job doesn't need production credentials, so it shouldn't be able to read them, reducing what's exposed if that job is ever compromised.

questions.q: What is the first step in rotating a JWT key pair used for CI authentication, per this lesson's sequence?
options: Immediately deactivate the old certificate before anything else
Delete the dedicated integration user and create a new one
Generate a new key pair and upload the new certificate to the Connected App, before touching the integration user's credentials at all
Change the org's My Domain URL
questions.explain: The sequence starts by generating and uploading a new certificate, updating the GitHub secret, confirming it works, and only then deactivating the old certificate -- so the pipeline is never left unable to authenticate mid-rotation.

questions.q: Who can view a GitHub Actions secret's value through the UI after it has been created?
options: Nobody -- a secret's value is write-only after creation; it can only be replaced, never viewed again
Any repository collaborator
Only the organization owner
Anyone with the repository's clone URL
questions.explain: Once created, a secret's value cannot be viewed again through GitHub's UI, by anyone, including admins -- it can only be overwritten with a new value.
